2082: Global commitments such as the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KM GBF) call for gender responsive conservation, yet marine governance continues to overlook women's roles, particularly in shark and ray capture and processing. Although women rarely participate in shark and ray capture, they play essential roles in pre-harvest preparation, post-harvest processing, and local trade in small-scale fisheries, while their involvement in commercial fisheries is concentrated in post-harvest work. Despite this, their potential contributions to shark and ray conservation remain poorly integrated into policy. This study draws on bycatch landing data in commercial bottom trawl fisheries (2019-2024), a socioeconomic survey (20222024), and qualitative interviews with key stakeholders to examine gendered labor dynamics in the wedgefish and guitarfish bycatch of Rembang District, Indonesia. Over 12,000 critically endangered individuals were recorded over five years, with more than 80% below maturity size, indicating severe conservation challenges. Men dominate vessel operations and make bycatchrelease decisions, but motivations differ: captains tend to release due to regulatory awareness, while crew members release very small individuals because their market value is negligible. In contrast, women processors often prefer smaller sharks and rays as they are easier to handle, smoke, and prepare for the local market, creating a gendered divergence in valuation and use of bycatch. Women sustain household economies through these microenterprises, yet their labor remains undervalued and excluded from governance. These findings underscore the need for gender-responsive management that recognizes women's contributions, addresses differing incentives across the value chain, and links livelihood security with effective elasmobranch conservation.

2086: Across the Western Indian Ocean (WIO), a broad body of scientific evidence, from BRUVS to fishers dialogues, catch-landing monitoring and two decades of underwater visual census data, demonstrates a sharp and ongoing decline in elasmobranch populations. Timed visual surveys reveal the near-absence of reef sharks across five WIO/Gulf of Aden countries, while catch assessments in Kenya show that 97% of landed sharks are juveniles and five of the eight commonly caught species are globally threatened. In Comoros, 70% of documented species fall within globally threatened categories. In parallel, several policy processes are gaining momentum. The IUCN SSG’s ISRA initiative has identified over key habitats for elasmobranchs across the WIO, providing tangible guidance for national spatial planning. Additionally, Kenya has developed a multi-stakeholder conservation strategy for threatened elasmobranchs, with potential as a replicable model mechanism for neighbouring states. However, policy uptake across the region remains slow and uneven. Data-sharing systems are weak, national actions are poorly aligned with regional frameworks, and some countries, particularly SIDS, lack the institutional capacity and political leverage to influence regional governance.In Comoros, the absence of dedicated legislation and a national red list for threatened elasmobranch species constrains the development of effective fishing regulations to reduce shark mortality. Consequently, scientific knowledge is advancing faster than policy mechanisms can absorb it. A coordinated regional approach is therefore essential. By exploring response strategies through policy processes to strengthen science-to-policy interfaces and harmonizing national efforts, WIO states can accelerate elasmobranch conservation and promote equitable implementation across diverse national contexts.

2089: Three decades of shark conservation in the Philippines reveal a dynamic interplay of science, policy, civil society, and sheer persistence. From fragmented data and opportunistic protection efforts in the late 1990s to today’s more comprehensive national frameworks and international commitments, the country’s journey has been marked by both milestones and missteps. This paper examines strategies that have begun to yield tangible results, highlighting the pivotal role of scientific evidence, legal instruments, multi-sectoral collaboration, sustained public engagement, and capacity building and training of law enforcers. Notable achievements include the legal protection of more than species, yet shark populations remain under significant pressure as new and emerging threats continue to challenge conservation gains. We underscore the urgent need for collective action, urging individuals and institutions to work together through the growing “Sharkada” movement to secure and sustain shark conservation in the Philippines.

2090: Global climate change is expected to intensify environmental variability in the world’s oceans, altering the predictability of habitats and the distribution of prey resources. These changes are particularly consequential for migratory marine predators whose movements and foraging success are tightly coupled to climate driven prey availability. In dynamic environments, like the open ocean, individuals may employ different behavioral strategies to optimize foraging success. Site fidelity, the tendency to return to a previously visited area, is one such strategy that may confer advantages by allowing individuals to exploit familiar habitats and resources. Salmon sharks (Lamna ditropis) exhibit broad-scale seasonal fidelity across the northeastern Pacific yet show high intraspecific variation in individual movement patterns. This combination of demonstrated capacity for fidelity and substantial individual variability makes them an ideal species for investigating how behavioral strategies are shaped by environmental stability. To gain insight into salmon shark movement and behavioral patterns, we deployed satellite position or temperature (SPOT) tags on females in Prince William Sound, Alaska, from 2003 to 2015. These tags recorded satellite positions for at least two years per individual. To identify behavioral strategies, we estimated annual home ranges using kernel utilization distributions. We then calculated overlap between years using Bhattacharyya’s coefficient to identify strong and weak fidelity strategies. Ongoing analyses integrate remotely sensed oceanographic data to evaluate the relationship between these strategies and environmental stability. This work provides insight into the adaptive capacity of salmon sharks and how behavioral variability may influence resilience to future environmental change.

2091: Basking sharks (Cetorhinus maximus) in Arctic waters have recently attracted more and welldeserved attention. They have been exploited in the past and little was known about their current distribution in the northern North Atlantic. The citizen science "shark hotline" was opened once again to provide real-time sightings data to enable the tagging of sharks with archival tags, as well as provided opportunities for plankton sampling, fisheries acoustics and hyperspectral imaging (from a plane and a fixed box on board) data collection to map plankton and especially Calanus abundances and ocean colour. 2092: Guitarfishes are among the most threatened elasmobranchs globally, with the widenose guitarfish (Glaucostegus obtusus) and sharpnose guitarfish (G. granulatus) listed as Critically Endangered. Despite their conservation status, limited ecological data and high fishery interactions hinder effective management in India. Over three years, we monitored coastal fisheries across a 1,911 km² area of Malvan, Maharashtra, documenting landings of more than elasmobranch species. Spatial analysis of catch records revealed disproportionately high captures of guitarfishes in three estuarine sand-flat systems situated in and around the Malvan Marine Sanctuary, suggesting the presence of key habitats such as nursery grounds and seasonal aggregation sites. Building on these insights, the current phase of the study focuses on understanding the population ecology, habitat use, and fishery overlap of G. obtusus and G. granulatus. We are conducting beach transect surveys to assess juvenile occurrence and seasonality, and mark–recapture experiments to estimate local population size and movement patterns. Feeding ecology is being examined through gut content analyses of both released and fishery-caught individuals to explore spatial differences in diet linked to habitat structure. These biological datasets will be integrated with fine-scale fishing effort and gear data to quantify spatial overlap and vulnerability to fishing pressure. In parallel, participatory outreach with fishers and local governance bodies aims to support knowledge-sharing and build stewardship. The outcomes of this research will provide a scientific evidence base for designing area-based management interventions, contributing to long-term conservation of guitarfishes along India’s west coast.

2096: Shark conservation in the Eastern Tropical Pacific (ETP) varies widely among countries, despite the region’s shared ecological importance and international commitments. This study evaluates the strength of national shark regulations across ten ETP countries by compiling all sharkrelated norms in force and assigning each country a protection score based on whether their legislation is conservation-oriented, mixed, or primarily fisheries-based. To understand how these legal frameworks translate into practice, we compared the protection score with two variables: participation in major international agreements and national exportation rates of shark products. The results show clear regional patterns. Finning bans and National Plans of Action for Sharks are common, but more robust measures—such as prohibiting targeted shark fishing—are implemented by only a few countries. Ecuador obtained the highest protection score, while Nicaragua and El Salvador ranked lowest. A positive correlation was found between participation in international agreements and stronger domestic frameworks. When incorporating exportation data, countries with lower protection scores tended to export more shark products or maintain less restrictive trade pathways, suggesting a gap between formal commitments and actual management outcomes. These results highlight the need to improve alignment between legal frameworks, export practices, and conservation objectives in the ETP. As a recommendation, future regional efforts could benefit from more consistent definitions of fisheries terms to reduce ambiguity, but the main finding remains the clear link between weak protection frameworks and higher export activity.

2098: Automation is key to scaling research beyond anecdotal data. Yet this remains challenging-especially for video-based surveys that produce large volumes of data. Once recorded, the central task is to extract relevant information before analysis can begin--typically through detection, classification when needed, tracking, and trajectory correction to maintain individual identities. This facilitates novel approaches to monitoring, conflict mitigation, and policy making. With TRex, we designed a software that supports each of these steps, enabling generalized, video-based, markerless multi-animal tracking--from small behavioral assays to thousands of individuals in large laboratory arenas, and drone surveys in the wild. The solution has been demonstrated to be effective with sharks, rays, and other similar systems. In this talk, I will highlight the potential of combining drones with automated analysis and introduce our open-source tool by demonstrating its capabilities and examples of successful applications in ongoing and completed studies. The talk is structured to convey practical insights beyond a single software solution, offering guidance for everyday research workflows from recording to analysis. Sensor proliferation shifts the bottleneck from collection to interpretation; our approach shows one adaptable way to meet this challenge in any data-rich field. As the world keeps moving towards quantitative studies across fields, let us not get left behind.

2101: In Kakinada, understanding sharks, rays, and rhino rays has meant sitting on boats, walking landing sites, and listening closely to fishers, traders, and other stakeholders who know these waters and the trade best. Between 2019 and 2025, we documented over 26,000 specimens, combining landing surveys with in-water observations as fisheries observers on single-day trips. This long-term engagement shows how a coastal community, already familiar with these species, adapted to changing policy, markets, and global attention. Onboard observations provided insights beyond landing-site surveys. Direct interaction with fishing operations revealed post-capture handling, incidental retention that often goes unrecorded, even before making it to the markets, and the actual catch per unit effort (CPUE) for different elasmobranchs. Observations allowed documentation of fishing locations, associated bycatch, and diverse operational contexts. They also revealed fisher attitudes, behaviours, speciesspecific knowledge, and constraints when handling large or protected species. These data highlight nuances of compliance, conservation awareness, and gaps between policy intent and fishery realities. Interactions with traders further exposed patterns in landing count and misses. End-of-day tallies often underestimate total harvest, missing redistributed catches, stocking patterns, and trade chains. These observations revealed the complexity of how sharks, rays, and rhino rays move through markets and how economic incentives and demand influence fisher behaviour and retention. This case study underscores the importance of trust, continuity, and collaboration. By partnering with fishers and traders, conservation gains both ecological insight and behavioural understanding, enabling interventions that reduce fishing mortality while supporting livelihoods.

2102: The California Current Large Marine Ecosystem (CCLME) is a highly productive upwelling zone of ecological and economic importance along the west coast of North America and is home to the broadnose sevengill shark (Notorynchus cepedianus; BSS), a large, high-order marine predator found in temperate coastal waters worldwide. Yet despite extensive research focused on the region’s fisheries, the ecological role of BSS remains poorly understood. We aim to address this knowledge gap by examining the movement and foraging ecology of BSS within the CCLME. Here we present results from acoustic monitoring (n = 80), stable isotope analysis (n = 329), and stomach content analysis using non-lethal lavage techniques (n = 59), conducted over a fouryear period in two CCLME estuarine regions (Willapa Bay and Puget Sound, Washington, USA). We provide evidence of high seasonal residency along with broader connectivity within the CCLME, as well as preliminary diet patterns indicating feeding at high trophic levels. Stomach content data reveal frequent predation on marine mammals and elasmobranchs, complemented by benthic prey such as crustaceans and demersal fishes, suggesting a flexible and opportunistic foraging strategy. Together with stable isotope values, these early results point to broad niche width and the potential for BSS to exert significant top-down influence across multiple habitat types. This work represents the first effort to characterize BSS foraging ecology within the CCLME and has important implications for ecosystem-based understanding along the U.S. West Coast, particularly as managers consider how apex predator dynamics shape productivity and trophic interactions within the region.

2103: Large marine predators play essential roles in pelagic ecosystems, shaping food webs through both direct predation and non-consumptive effects. However, the size-structured nature of these interactions remains poorly understood, particularly for pelagic sharks whose early life stages are rarely observed. Unlike many coastal species that use well-defined nurseries, juvenile pelagic sharks occupy vast, dynamic environments where prey availability and predation risk are difficult to quantify. Using a large dataset of over 19,000 individual length estimates derived from 1,860 mid-water baited remote underwater video systems deployments across three ocean basins, we investigate the size distributions of sympatric wildlife associated with blue Prionace glauca, silky Carcharhinus falciformis, shortfin mako Isurus oxyrinchus, and dusky Carcharhinus obscurus sharks across their ontogenies. We compare absolute and relative sizes of associated fauna to determine whether juveniles and adult sharks occur with distinct community size structures, and assess how gape limitation influences access to prey resources. By classifying wildlife into juvenile-prey, adult-prey, and non-prey size categories, we construct “pelagic preyscapes” that reveal insights into how prey availability and predation risk may shift throughout life stages. Our findings offer rare empirical insights into early life stage ecology in pelagic sharks and demonstrate the central role of body size in shaping ecological interactions, highlight the importance of integrating size structure and ontogeny into conservation planning and developing size-explicit benchmarks for monitoring.
2104: The daisy stingray inhabits coastal waters of the African countries bordering the Atlantic Ocean. In Benin, this species is mainly fished by the artisanal fleet with occasional landings by the semi-industrial fleet. This species is caught along with other commercial species by the main gears operated in the coastal waters. Its permanent occurrence in the gears of all mesh sizes has led to questions about the current status of the stock in Benin, where no management plan exists for elasmobranchs. Demography, exploitation, and current stock status parameters of the daisy stingray have been estimated using the ELEFAN routine improved by a genetic algorithm, ELEFAN_GA, embedded in the R package TropFishR. The length-converted catch curve and the length-based yield-per-recruit model have been employed. 2105: Chondrichthyans are among the most vulnerable deep-sea fauna in the Northern Indian Ocean. The deep-sea surveys conducted by FORV Sagar Sampada under CMLRE between 2008 and 2018 reveal the distinct spatial patterns in chondrichthyan assemblages across the Andaman Sea, the southeastern Arabian Sea, and the Bay of Bengal. Using EXPO model trawls and HighSpeed Demersal Trawls, the surveys recorded a wide range of taxa from to 1262 m depth. Species composition varied markedly by region, with Centrophorus spp., Plesiobatis daviesi, and Hydrolagus spp. dominating the Andaman Sea, whereas the southeastern Arabian Sea yielded a richer assemblage including Apristurus, Etmopterus, Centroselachus crepidater, Neoharriotta pinnata, Rhinochimaera sp., and Hydrolagus africanus. The Terrace off Trivandrum, sampled extensively in 2013, exhibited the highest species richness and biomass, particularly among deep-water chimaeras (Hydrolagus, Hariotta, Rhinochimaera) and rays (Benthobatis, Dipturus), underscoring the ecological significance of bathyal habitats beyond 1000 m. High biomass records of Centrophorus sp. and Benthobatis moresbyi further suggest the presence of dense populations within specific depth strata. It also documents significant discoveries, including five new records, three new geographic range extensions, and two newly established depth records. Although research on chondrichthyan diversity has advanced considerably in the past decade with the adoption of modern technologies, these findings further underscore the abundance and ecological significance of deep-sea chondrichthyans in the Northern Indian Ocean and highlights the persistent challenges in species identification and the need for continued exploration in the region.

2106: In this study, we describe the migrations and behaviour of porbeagles (Lamna nasus, range 91-265cm) caught in the Celtic Sea, the west of Ireland and the Bay of Biscay and tagged with pop-up satellite tags (PSAT). During summer, porbeagles occupied warm stratified waters, diving between the surface and depths of up to 200m, remaining close to productive fronts. As the year progressed, the mean and maximum depths that porbeagles used increased as they migrated south into waters over the continental slope (>200m and up to 1400m), showing no clear pattern of association with frontal systems. Porbeagles showed a strong diel pattern of depth occupation, occurring in deeper water by day than during the night. This pattern was particularly evident during the winter, when porbeagle moved beyond 200m and foraged at the deep scattering layer by day. During this time, the majority of porbeagles resided in the region of the Bay of Biscay, although one porbeagle moved west to the mid-Atlantic ridge, and another migrated into the North Sea. Those porbeagles at liberty for more than months typically returned to the area of tagging. Our results provide strong evidence of long-distance migration and flexible foraging behaviours, as well as strengthening evidence for a general north to south migration of porbeagles in the NE Atlantic that relates to the development of productive frontal systems during the summer months.

2108: The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (KSA) has territorial waters in both the Red Sea and the Arabian Gulf; two regions that have been subject to limited study and declining elasmobranch populations. 2112: For years (2011-2021) we flew an aerial survey along the shoreline of southeast Florida, USA, to quantify seasonal abundance of blacktip sharks, Carcharhinus limbatus. A video camera recorded a field of view from the shoreline to approximately 200m offshore along a transect from Boca Raton Inlet to Jupiter Inlet (2011-2014) or Government Cut Miami to Jupiter Inlet (2015-2021). Blacktip sharks overwinter in southeast Florida from about January to April with a peak in abundance during mid- February. Mean water temperature during those months increased 1˚ C over the study period while mean shark abundance declined significantly. Peak shark abundance between Boca Raton Inlet and Jupiter Inlet exceeded 12,000 sharks in 2011, but did not exceed 1,200 sharks in 2021. Shark density differed significantly along the transect with the greatest density of sharks occurring in the northernmost sections. For the first four years of the study (2011-2014) sharks were found in the greatest density between Boynton Beach Inlet and Palm Beach Inlet. In subsequent years (2015-2020) the greatest density occurred farther north, between Palm Beach Inlet and Jupiter Inlet. This suggests a shift to a more northern distribution. As global water temperatures continue to rise, sharks will likely be found at increasingly higher latitudes to remain within their preferred temperature range. Departure of sharks from their overwintering grounds was strongly correlated with increasing photoperiod, which, along with rising water temperature, might act as a cue to initiate northward migration.

2113: Elasmobranchs are among the most threatened vertebrate groups worldwide, yet conservation and management remain limited by fragmented and geographically uneven data. Addressing these gaps requires a structured approach to identify and prioritise research needs; this is essential where financial and logistical resources are limited. The SharkScape project responds to this challenge by developing a generalisable research-priority framework for nine focal species, presented here using the central and northern North Sea, Orkney, and Shetland as a case study. We undertook a systematic literature review to identify knowledge gaps across lifehistory, ecological, genetic, and management domains. Spatial datasets from fisheries surveys, tagging programmes, industry sources, and citizen science initiatives were standardised, validated, and mapped to establish confirmed presence across regional and local scales. In parallel, a structured gap analysis organised the literature by species, topic, and geographic coverage to determine where biological and ecological information was lacking. To prioritise these gaps, we developed a Biological Vulnerability Index integrating life-history, ecological, and genetic traits, alongside a four-tier framework ranking research parameters by their management value. Feasibility was incorporated through a presence-weighting factor, ensuring that priority gaps were only elevated where species occur often enough to support viable research. Finally, we aligned biological priorities with conservation status and listing frameworks to integrate intrinsic vulnerability with existing or emerging policy obligations. Together, this framework provides a transparent and transferable approach for identifying high-impact evidence needs and demonstrates how priority gaps can vary across spatial scales, offering a robust foundation for targeted research and conservation planning.

2119: Maintaining buoyancy is essential for many aquatic species to regulate their vertical position in the water column. While most pelagic fishes have a swim bladder that can be adjusted to regulate buoyancy, sharks lack such a gas-filled organ. Most species are negatively buoyant and only rely on their large lipid-rich liver and active locomotion to generate lift. Carcharias taurus, a large shark distributed in coastal waters worldwide, is the only shark species known to gulp atmospheric air to hold in their stomachs. Although this behavior has been speculated to provide buoyancy control, the underlying drivers and implications of this behavior have not been investigated. Our study assessed the prevalence of air gulping in Carcharias taurus and the energetic and behavioral consequences of this behavior, especially regarding buoyancy control. To this end, eight C. taurus individuals were fitted with high-resolution acceleration data loggers in Delaware, USA, for periods of 1-4 days. Body posture and relative energetic expenditure were estimated from the acceleration data and used to assess buoyancy dynamics following the gulping events recorded. Movement metrics such as tailbeat period and path tortuosity were derived and used to classify discrete behavioral phases to investigate the behavioral implications of gulping. Preliminary data revealed a steep increase in buoyancy following gulping events, and that C. taurus can retain gulped air in their stomach for at least hours. These results support our hypothesis that air gulping by C. taurus is a unique strategy to perform buoyancy control among sharks.

2120: Insufficient data is a major challenge in conservation, particularly in the Eastern Mediterranean where research and historical records are scarce. Citizen science offers an efficient, costeffective, and non-intrusive tool for gathering information on species abundance, trends, and distributions. This study compiled photographed encounters of elasmobranchs along the shallow Israeli coast (0–40 m), reported between 2014–2023 by divers, fishermen, and other sea enthusiasts. Each verified observation was added to a database with date, location, species, sex, reproduction status, and environmental details. Around contributors reported 5,400 observations of five shark and seventeen ray species. We identified a gradual shift in community composition from south to north, likely driven by habitat differences. Distinct seasonal patterns emerged, with some species aggregating mainly in spring (e.g., Dasyatis pastinaca), others more common in autumn (e.g., Aetomylaeus bovinus, Rhinoptera marginata), and some present year-round (e.g., Taeniurops grabatus, Himantura spp.). Temporal trends over the past decade suggest possible recovery in several species, while others showed no clear increase. This study provides the first regional-scale description of species composition, seasonal distribution, and temporal dynamics along the Israeli coast, revealing a community structure distinct from the Western Mediterranean and supporting the identification of key sites for protection, such as reproduction and aggregation areas.

2130: Reef-associated shark populations have strongly declined globally, mainly due to fisheries and habitat degradation. In large parts of the Caribbean, status and movement ecology of shark species that use coral reefs during at least one life stage remain largely unknown. This longterm study focuses on tracking individual behaviour of reef-associated sharks with acoustic telemetry to determine their movement ecology at different scales. A network of acoustic receivers was deployed on the reefs around Saba, St Eustatius, St Maarten and the Saba Bank in the northeast Caribbean. Small marine parks are present around Saba, St Eustatius and St Maarten. The large “Yarari” marine mammal and shark sanctuary encompasses the Saba Bank, Saba, St Eustatius reefs and the pelagic waters in between these reefs. Since 2014, sharks were implanted with acoustic transmitters (V16/V16p, InnovaSea): Caribbean Reef Shark Carcharhinus perezi, Nurse Shark Ginglymostoma cirratum, Tiger Shark Galeocerdo cuvier and Silky Shark Carcharhinus falciformis. Juvenile and adult Caribbean reef sharks, and juvenile nurse sharks showed strong residency within relatively small home ranges. Juvenile silky sharks mainly occupied one site on the Saba Bank. adult nurse sharks and juvenile tiger sharks showed higher mobility and shorter lasting residency. Larger scale movements between reefs separated by deep waters (>500m) were observed for adult Caribbean Reef sharks, often short and directed back-and-forth trips, juvenile silky sharks, adult nurse sharks and juvenile tiger sharks. The results of this study have implications for assessing the effectiveness of marine protected areas.

2132: Sharks are apex predators that play a vital role in structuring marine ecosystems, yet their populations are increasingly threatened by anthropogenic stressors such as fishing, pollutants, and habitat degradation. Traditional measures of stress in sharks have relied on corticosteroids, but these are difficult to quantify in elasmobranchs, emphasizing the need for alternative biomarkers. We investigated stress physiology in four species that inhabit a highly urbanized estuarine system, Tampa Bay: Bonnethead Shark (Sphyrna tiburo), Blacknose Shark (Carcharhinus acronotus), Blacktip Shark (Carcharhinus limbatus), and Atlantic Sharpnose Shark (Rhizoprionodon terraenovae). Plasma samples were analyzed for metabolic (ketones) and oxidative (malondialdehyde) stress markers, and compared to proteome profiles generated by LC-MS/MS (Mass spectrometry). We identified over proteins, including acute phase proteins, enzymes involved in glycolysis and gluconeogenesis, and proteins linked to lipid and biotin metabolism. Principal component analysis revealed species-, size-, and sex-specific proteomic variation, with several proteins significantly correlated with ketone and oxidized lipid levels. These findings provide the first plasma proteome profiles for these four shark species, identify candidate protein biomarkers of metabolic and oxidative stress, and suggest physiological mechanisms that may underlie differences in life history and ecological resilience. Our results establish a foundation for developing non-lethal, protein-based metrics of shark health in disturbed coastal ecosystems.
2133: Sharks, rays, and skates (elasmobranchs) are experiencing global population declines, leading to increasing concern over the impacts of target fishing and bycatch on their populations. Globally, elasmobranchs are often sold under general or misleading seafood labels, leading to confusion about species identity and often inhibits proper enforcement and traceability for these species along the seafood supply chain. Therefore, it is important to increase transparency about the identity of species sold to address the potential impact of mislabeled or illegally harvested threatened elasmobranchs.We performed DNA barcode sequencing to identify the composition of rays sold in markets in La Paz, Baja California Sur, Mexico. We identified samples collected between 2020-2022 representing species belonging to eight families. None of the samples were accurately labeled to the species level, and were instead sold under four categories: mantarraya, pescado seco, machaca, and cubana seca. The most common species identified by genetic analyses were diamond stingray (Hypanus dipterurus), longtail stingray (H. longus), and California butterfly ray (Gymnura marmorata). Greater than 78% of the samples surveyed are considered threatened by the IUCN Red List. Among these were two species of devil ray (Mobula munkiana and M. thurstoni), both of which are federally protected in Mexico. We recommend expanding point of purchase identification for fresh products weighed and packaged in markets with Mexican authorities to better understand the extent of elasmobranch fishing.

2139: Sharks and rays are ecologically important species in the wider North Sea ecosystem, and although several species historically occurred throughout the Dutch Continental Shelf (DCS), major knowledge gaps remain regarding their movement ecology, habitat use and ecological roles. Addressing these knowledge gaps, as required under the North Sea Agreement, provides a basis for more effective management of the wider North Sea ecosystem. The MONS Shark and Ray Research program (2025-2028) addresses two major knowledge gaps: the movement ecology and habitat use of sharks and rays, and the trophic ecology and ecological role of sharks and rays. To study the movement ecology and habitat use of sharks and rays we combine telemetry (acoustic, data-storage, and pop-up archival tags) and fisheries-independent surveys to: determine long-distance movements between the DCS and adjacent waters, fine-scale movements in coastal areas, estuaries and offshore wind farms, and determine the function of specific areas as (seasonal) nursery or feeding areas for different life stages. To address knowledge gaps in the trophic ecology of sharks and rays, we use a combination of techniques (stable isotope analysis, diet metabarcoding and stomach content analysis) to determine how trophic niches, food web positions, and diet change across species and life stages. We integrate this information with the movement ecology and the ecomorphological traits of these species to determine to what extent diet drives movement and habitat use. By resolving these interconnected knowledge gaps, this research program provides the ecological insights needed for evidence-based management of a rapidly changing North Sea

2143: The broadnose sevengill shark, Notorynchus cepedianus, is a coastal apex predator considered Critically Endangered in Brazil, with limited recent data on its occurrence. In October 2025, new records were documented at Cassino Beach, Rio Grande, Rio Grande do Sul State, through verified reports from recreational fishers and local observers engaged in beach monitoring activities. Five confirmed events were registered, including three individuals captured by rod and line and released alive, and two stranded specimens found dead on the beach. Photographic and video evidence enabled accurate species identification, and the largest individual measured approximately cm in total length, indicating that juveniles and subadults use these shallow nearshore waters. These reports were voluntarily submitted through the social media network of Projeto Tubarão, demonstrating how digital platforms can facilitate rapid communication, strengthen trust between scientists and fishing communities, and overcome longstanding barriers that have historically limited collaborative research. Although the broader trajectory of Projeto Tubarão is beyond the scope of this study, its established network across multiple Brazilian states, played a pivotal role in enabling fishers to proactively share reliable information, reinforcing collaborative monitoring efforts. Our findings confirm the persistence of N. cepedianus in the cold, high-productivity coastal waters of southern Brazil and extend the temporal window of confirmed occurrence for the species in the southwestern Atlantic. This collaborative approach between scientists and local fishers highlights the growing importance of participatory monitoring as a complementary tool for enhancing species assessments, guiding conservation priorities, and improving data availability in data-poor regions.

2145: Implementation of CITES listings for shark and ray species has expanded rapidly over the past decade, with increased listings, creating an urgent need for efficient, standardised, and scientifically robust Non-Detriment Findings (NDFs) to inform authorities of the potential for trade. To support Parties in meeting these obligations, the electronic Non-Detriment Finding (e-NDF) software tool has been developed. 2151: Chondrichthyans and their parasites represent one of the most ancient host-parasite systems on the planet with a co-evolution that exists for more than million years. The dorsum of N. brasiliensis is characterised by dark horizontal blotches patterned as bands along the disc, with emphasis on the blotch on the rostrum and at the base of each dorsal fin, without spots in any region of the body. Sharks, rays, and chimaeras are classified in the class Chondrichthyes, a monophyletic group and the sister group of Osteichthyes. In this class, the heart is composed of four chambers: the atrium, ventricle, sinus venosus, and conus arteriosus. Within the conus arteriosus there is a variable number of valves that prevent blood backflow during diastole. The number and arrangement of the valves vary among species, which may be related to phylogenetic issues. Descriptions of the heart chambers have been made for some taxa, but there is a scarcity of data for certain genera and orders. This work investigates the morphological variation of the conus arteriosus and its valves, encompassing different groups, to survey characters for phylogenetic and ecomorphological inferences. A total of 98 hearts from 13 of the 14 orders currently recognised for Chondrichthyes were examined. Manual dissections were performed to remove the hearts, which were stored in 70% alcohol, from specimens in collections. Subsequently, incisions were made at the side and the upper and lower ends of the conus of each heart to observe the valves. The hearts were stained with alcian blue for better visualisation of the structures, and photographs were taken with an auto-montage stereomicroscope. Variations in the number of rows and columns of valves, as well as their shape and distribution along the conus, were observed. Among the characters already surveyed is the pattern of distribution of the valves along the length of the conus, which may be present from the posterior to the anterior portion, as occurs in Carcharhinus obscurus, or absent in the anterior portion of the conus, as in Squalus albicaudus. Analyses are still under way and more characters will be proposed, so that a better understanding of the evolution and functional morphology of characters associated with the heart, the conus, and its valves can be obtained.
